taxonomyNote: NatureServe and ADW include three subspecies (chrysea, miaria, reticularia) within the species.
fieldMarks: Identified by a very long, yellow-striped neck, about as long as the plastron and up to 80% of carapace length.
Pear-shaped, olive to dark brown carapace with a reticulate network of yellow to orange lines; solid yellow plastron; yellow stripes on the legs.
Carapace 15.3-17.8 cm typically, to 25.4 cm; females about 1.5 times larger than males; males have thicker tails, longer front claws and a more compressed shell.
behavior: Diurnal and often seen on land migrating between wetlands or seeking soil to burrow into; land activity in South Carolina peaks in March and April; basks, and is wary when basking.
Hibernates in mud and vegetation in the north of its range; Florida animals stay active all year; may aestivate on land when wetlands dry.
Eats crustaceans, aquatic insects, tadpoles, fish and plants, using suction feeding; nests August-September and February-March in South Carolina.
habitat: Shallow ponds and lakes with thick vegetation, cypress swamps, ditches and temporary pools, usually not flowing water; wanders overland, especially in spring.
range: Southeastern and south-central US coastal plain; NatureServe lists Virginia, North and South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Arkansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas; not recorded for Canada.
